title: 128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)
stop: The officer stops asking once the applicant has answered 12 correctly or missed 9.
who: For applicants who file Form N-400 on or after October 20, 2025.

senior.text: Applicants 65 or older who have been lawful permanent residents for 20 or more years may study just the 20 questions marked with an asterisk (*). The officer asks 10 of them, and 6 correct passes. They may take the civics test in the language of their choice.

intro: Listed below are the 128 civics questions and answers for the 2025 version of the civics test. These questions cover important topics about American government and history. The civics test is an oral test and the USCIS officer will ask you to answer up to 20 out of the 128 civics test questions. You must answer at least 12 questions correctly to pass the 2025 version of the civics test.
Although USCIS is aware that there may be additional correct answers to the civics questions, applicants are encouraged to respond to the questions using the answers provided below.

On the civics test, some answers may change because of elections or appointments. Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates to find any answers that may have changed on the civics test. You must answer the question with the name of the official serving at the time of your naturalization interview.

sources.name: USCIS, "128 Civics Questions and Answers (2025 version)", M-1778 (09/25) (official PDF)

CitizenIQ, "All 128 USCIS Civics Questions and Answers (2025)" (transcription B)

questions.q: What is the form of government of the United States?
questions.idea: The United States is a republic: the people elect representatives to make laws for them, and there is no king. It is also a federal republic, because power is shared between the national government and the states, and it is based on a written Constitution. Memory hook: a republic is “representatives, not royalty.”

questions.q: What is the supreme law of the land?
questions.idea: The Constitution is the highest law in the country. Every other law, federal or state, must agree with it, and a law that goes against it can be struck down by the courts. Article VI calls it “the supreme Law of the Land.” Memory hook: the Constitution sits at the top of the ladder of laws.

questions.q: Name one thing the U.S. Constitution does.
a: Protects the rights of the people
questions.idea: The Constitution sets up the government and divides it into three branches. It says what each branch may do and puts limits on its power. With its amendments, it also protects the rights of the people. It was written in 1787 and took effect in 1789.

questions.q: The U.S. Constitution starts with the words “We the People.” What does “We the People” mean?
questions.idea: “We the People” are the first words of the Constitution. They mean the government gets its power from the people, not from a king. This idea is called popular sovereignty, or consent of the governed. The people agree to be governed, which is the idea of the social contract.

questions.q: How are changes made to the U.S. Constitution?
questions.idea: The Constitution is changed by amendments. An amendment is usually proposed by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and must then be ratified by three-fourths of the states. Article V describes this process. It was made hard on purpose, so that the basic law changes only when most of the country agrees.

questions.q: What does the Bill of Rights protect?
a: (The basic) rights of people living in the United States
questions.idea: The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments to the Constitution, added in 1791. It protects basic rights such as freedom of speech, freedom of religion and the right to a fair trial. Many of these rights protect everyone living in the United States, not only citizens.

questions.q: How many amendments does the U.S. Constitution have?
questions.idea: The Constitution has 27 amendments, or changes. The first ten, the Bill of Rights, were added together in 1791. The most recent, the 27th, took effect in 1992 and is about pay raises for members of Congress. Amending is hard on purpose, so it has happened only 27 times in more than 230 years.

questions.q: Why is the Declaration of Independence important?
a: It says America is free from British control.
It says all people are created equal.
questions.idea: The Declaration of Independence explained why the colonies were breaking away from Britain. It says all people are created equal and have rights that no government gives and none may take away, such as life and liberty. These ideas have been quoted by Americans ever since, from Abraham Lincoln to Martin Luther King, Jr.

questions.q: What founding document said the American colonies were free from Britain?
questions.idea: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on July 4, 1776. It told the world that the thirteen colonies were now free and independent states, no longer ruled by Great Britain. It also gave the reasons: people have rights, and a government that destroys those rights loses its claim to rule.

questions.q: Name two important ideas from the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
questions.idea: These ideas come from both founding documents. The Declaration says people are equal and have natural rights. The Constitution sets up a limited government run by the people themselves. The social contract means people agree to form a government to protect their rights. Name any two from the list.

questions.q: The words “Life, Liberty, and the pursuit of Happiness” are in what founding document?
questions.idea: These famous words are from the Declaration of Independence (1776), not the Constitution. They name rights that the Declaration calls “unalienable,” meaning they cannot be taken away. Memory hook: the Declaration declares rights; the Constitution constructs the government.

questions.q: What is the economic system of the United States?
questions.idea: The United States has a capitalist, or free market, economy. Most businesses are owned by private people, and prices are set mostly by buying and selling. Government still makes rules, such as laws about safety and fair dealing, and collects taxes.

questions.q: What is the rule of law?
a: No one is above the law.
questions.idea: The rule of law means the same laws apply to everyone, including the people who make and enforce them. Leaders cannot simply do what they want; they must follow the law like anyone else. Memory hook: “No one is above the law.”

questions.q: Many documents influenced the U.S. Constitution. Name one.
questions.idea: The writers of the Constitution learned from earlier documents. The Mayflower Compact (1620) and the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut (1639) were early plans for self-government; the Virginia Declaration of Rights (1776) listed rights; the Articles of Confederation (1781) were the first national plan. Some historians also point to the Iroquois Great Law of Peace, though they debate how much it shaped the Constitution. Any one of these is correct.

questions.q: There are three branches of government. Why?
a: So one part does not become too powerful
questions.idea: The writers of the Constitution feared that power in one set of hands could become tyranny. So they split the government into three branches, each with its own job. Each branch can check the others. This is called separation of powers and checks and balances.

questions.q: Name the three branches of government.
questions.idea: The three branches are the legislative branch (Congress), which makes laws; the executive branch (the President), which carries them out; and the judicial branch (the courts), which explains them. Memory hook: make, carry out, explain. Articles I, II and III of the Constitution set up the three branches in that order.

questions.q: The President of the United States is in charge of which branch of government?
questions.idea: The President is the head of the executive branch. That branch carries out and enforces the laws. It includes the Vice President, the Cabinet and the federal departments and agencies.

questions.q: What part of the federal government writes laws?
questions.idea: Congress is the legislative branch, and its main job is to write laws. Article I of the Constitution gives “all legislative powers” to Congress. “Legislature” means a law-making body.

questions.q: What are the two parts of the U.S. Congress?
questions.idea: Congress has two parts, or “houses”: the Senate and the House of Representatives. A bill must pass both before it goes to the President. This two-house design is called a bicameral legislature. It came from the Great Compromise of 1787.

questions.q: Name one power of the U.S. Congress.
questions.idea: Article I gives Congress its powers. It writes the laws, decides how the government raises and spends money (the federal budget), and has the power to declare war. It also can collect taxes, borrow money and regulate trade between states.

questions.q: How many U.S. senators are there?
questions.idea: Each of the 50 states has two senators, so there are 100 in all. Every state gets the same number, no matter how many people live there. Memory hook: 50 states × 2 = 100.

questions.q: How long is a term for a U.S. senator?
questions.idea: Senators serve six-year terms. The terms are staggered: about one third of the Senate is elected every two years. The long term lets senators take a longer view, and the staggering means the whole Senate never changes at once.

questions.q: Who is one of your state’s U.S. senators now?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents and residents of U.S. territories should answer that D.C. (or the territory where the applicant lives) has no U.S. senators.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on where you live, and it changes after elections. To find your two senators, go to senate.gov and choose your state, or see USCIS’s page uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. Give the name of a senator serving on the day of your interview. People in Washington, D.C., and the U.S. territories have no U.S. senators, and saying so is the right answer for them.

questions.q: How many voting members are in the House of Representatives?
questions.idea: The House of Representatives has 435 voting members. Congress fixed that number by law, and it has stayed at 435 for most of the time since 1913. Seats are divided among the states by population, so big states have many representatives and small states may have only one. Washington, D.C., and the territories send delegates who cannot vote on the final passage of bills.

questions.q: How long is a term for a member of the House of Representatives?
questions.idea: Members of the House serve two-year terms, so every seat is on the ballot every even-numbered year. The short term keeps representatives close to the voters, who can quickly keep them or replace them.

questions.q: Why do U.S. representatives serve shorter terms than U.S. senators?
a: To more closely follow public opinion
questions.idea: Representatives face the voters every two years, but senators only every six. Because of this, House members must pay close attention to what the people want right now. The founders wanted one house that would follow public opinion closely and one that would be steadier.

questions.q: How many senators does each state have?
questions.idea: Every state has two senators. This gives each state an equal voice in the Senate, whether it is large or small. In the House, by contrast, the number of members depends on population.

questions.q: Why does each state have two senators?
questions.idea: At the Constitutional Convention in 1787, large states wanted representation by population and small states wanted equal votes. The Great Compromise, also called the Connecticut Compromise, gave them both: the House is based on population, and the Senate gives every state two seats. This protects the voice of small states.

questions.q: Name your U.S. representative.
a: Answers will vary. [Residents of territories with nonvoting Delegates or Resident Commissioners may provide the name of that Delegate or Commissioner. Also acceptable is any statement that the territory has no (voting) representatives in Congress.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on your address, and it changes after elections. Go to house.gov and use “Find Your Representative” with your ZIP code, or see uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. Give the name of the person serving on the day of your interview. People in territories with a nonvoting delegate or resident commissioner may name that person.

questions.q: What is the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
questions.idea: This answer can change at any time the House chooses a new Speaker, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it before your interview. The Speaker is elected by the members of the House to lead it, and comes right after the Vice President in the line of succession to the presidency.

questions.q: Who does a U.S. senator represent?
questions.idea: A U.S. senator represents everyone in his or her state, not just one district. That is why a senator must think about the whole state, its cities and its countryside.

questions.q: Who elects U.S. senators?
questions.idea: Senators are elected by the voters of their state. At first, state legislatures chose senators. The 17th Amendment, added in 1913, gave that choice directly to the people.

questions.q: Who does a member of the House of Representatives represent?
questions.idea: Each state is divided into congressional districts, with about the same number of people in each. A member of the House represents the people of one district. A state with only one representative is one big district.

questions.q: Who elects members of the House of Representatives?
questions.idea: The voters who live in a congressional district elect its member of the House. Elections for every House seat are held every two years, in November of even-numbered years.

questions.q: Some states have more representatives than other states. Why?
questions.idea: Seats in the House are shared out by population. After each census, taken every ten years, the seats are divided again, so states that grow can gain seats and others can lose them. This is called apportionment. The Senate is different: every state has two senators.

questions.q: The President of the United States is elected for how many years?
questions.idea: The President is elected for a four-year term. Presidential elections are held every four years, in years that can be divided by four, like 2024 and 2028. Since the 22nd Amendment, a President can be elected only twice.

questions.q: The President of the United States can serve only two terms. Why?
a: To keep the president from becoming too powerful
questions.idea: The 22nd Amendment, added in 1951, says no one may be elected President more than twice. George Washington set the custom of serving only two terms. Franklin Roosevelt was elected four times, and afterward the country made the two-term limit part of the Constitution, to keep any President from becoming too powerful.

questions.q: What is the name of the President of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the President of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes with elections, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it shortly before your interview. Give the name of the person who is President on the day of your interview. The President is elected every four years and takes office on January 20.

questions.q: What is the name of the Vice President of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Vice President of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes with elections, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates; check it before your interview. The Vice President is elected together with the President, on the same ticket, and also serves as President of the Senate.

questions.q: If the president can no longer serve, who becomes president?
a: The Vice President (of the United States)
questions.idea: If the President dies, resigns or is removed from office, the Vice President becomes President. The 25th Amendment, added in 1967, made this rule clear. This has happened nine times in American history.

questions.q: Name one power of the president.
questions.idea: The Constitution gives the President several powers. The President signs or vetoes bills, enforces the laws, commands the military, leads relations with other countries and appoints federal judges, with the Senate’s approval. Name any one of these.

questions.q: Who is Commander in Chief of the U.S. military?
questions.idea: The Constitution makes the President the Commander in Chief of the Army and Navy, which today means all the armed forces. This puts the military under the control of an elected civilian. Congress still holds the power to declare war and to pay for the military.

questions.q: Who signs bills to become laws?
questions.idea: After both houses of Congress pass a bill, it goes to the President. If the President signs it, it becomes law. This is one of the checks between the branches: Congress writes the law, and the President must agree, or Congress must override a veto.

questions.q: Who vetoes bills?
questions.idea: A veto is the President’s refusal to sign a bill. The word is Latin for “I forbid.” Congress can still make the bill a law if two-thirds of the House and two-thirds of the Senate vote to override the veto. This is a clear example of checks and balances.

questions.q: Who appoints federal judges?
questions.idea: The President nominates federal judges, including Supreme Court justices. The Senate must then approve, or confirm, them. Sharing this power between two branches is another check and balance.

questions.q: The executive branch has many parts. Name one.
questions.idea: The executive branch is large. It includes the President, the Vice President, the Cabinet and many federal departments and agencies, such as the Department of State and the Department of the Treasury. These offices carry out the laws that Congress passes.

questions.q: What does the President’s Cabinet do?
a: Advises the President (of the United States)
questions.idea: The Cabinet is the group of top advisers to the President, mostly the heads of the big executive departments, such as the Secretary of State and the Attorney General. They advise the President and run their departments. The Constitution mentions the heads of departments giving their opinions in writing; the custom of meeting as a Cabinet began with George Washington.

questions.q: What are two Cabinet-level positions?
a: Secretary of Health and Human Services
Secretary of Housing and Urban Development
Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency
Administrator of the Small Business Administration
Director of the Central Intelligence Agency
Director of the Office of Management and Budget
questions.idea: The Cabinet includes the heads of the 15 executive departments, such as the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury and the Attorney General, plus the Vice President and some other officials the President gives Cabinet rank. The Department of Defense was called the War Department until after World War II, so the list accepts either name. Memorize two that are easy for you, such as Secretary of State and Attorney General.

questions.q: Why is the Electoral College important?
a: It decides who is elected president.
It provides a compromise between the popular election of the president and congressional selection.
questions.idea: Americans do not vote for President directly. Each state chooses electors, equal to its number of senators and representatives, and the electors cast the votes that elect the President. There are 538 electors, and a candidate needs 270 to win. The founders created this system as a compromise between letting Congress choose and a direct popular vote.

questions.q: What is one part of the judicial branch?
questions.idea: The judicial branch is made up of the courts. The Supreme Court is at the top, and below it are the lower federal courts that Congress has created, such as district courts and courts of appeals. Name either part.

questions.q: What does the judicial branch do?
a: Decides if a law goes against the (U.S.) Constitution
questions.idea: Courts settle disputes about the law and explain what laws mean. They can also decide whether a law goes against the Constitution; this is called judicial review. The Supreme Court confirmed this power in the case Marbury v. Madison in 1803.

questions.q: What is the highest court in the United States?
questions.idea: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. It is the only court the Constitution names; Congress created the lower federal courts. Its decisions on the Constitution and federal law are final for all other courts. It meets in Washington, D.C.

questions.q: How many seats are on the Supreme Court?
questions.idea: The Supreme Court has nine seats: one Chief Justice and eight Associate Justices. The Constitution does not set the number; Congress does, by law. It has been nine since 1869.

questions.q: How many Supreme Court justices are usually needed to decide a case?
questions.idea: The Supreme Court decides cases by majority vote. With nine justices, a majority is five. Memory hook: five of nine is more than half.

questions.q: How long do Supreme Court justices serve?
questions.idea: Federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, serve “during good behaviour,” in the words of Article III. In practice this means for life, unless they retire, resign or are removed by impeachment. Their pay also cannot be cut while they serve.

questions.q: Supreme Court justices serve for life. Why?
questions.idea: Lifetime terms let judges decide cases by the law without worrying about losing their jobs. They do not have to run for election or please a President or Congress. This is meant to keep the courts independent of politics.

questions.q: Who is the Chief Justice of the United States now?
a: Visit uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates for the name of the Chief Justice of the United States.
questions.idea: This answer changes when a new Chief Justice is appointed, so this page does not print a name. USCIS keeps the current answer at uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates. The Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court and is chosen by the President with the approval of the Senate. Like the other justices, the Chief Justice serves for life.

questions.q: Name one power that is only for the federal government.
questions.idea: The Constitution gives some powers only to the national government, so the country speaks with one voice. Only the federal government may print money, mint coins, declare war, build an army, make treaties and set foreign policy. Article I, Section 10, forbids the states from doing several of these things.

questions.q: Name one power that is only for the states.
questions.idea: Under federalism, the states keep powers that the Constitution does not give to the national government. States run public schools, police and fire protection, driver’s licenses and decisions about how land is used. These powers touch daily life, so state and local government matter a great deal.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 10th Amendment?
a: (It states that the) powers not given to the federal government belong to the states or to the people.
questions.idea: The 10th Amendment says powers not given to the federal government by the Constitution, and not forbidden to the states, belong to the states or to the people. It reminds everyone that the national government has only the powers the Constitution lists.

questions.q: Who is the governor of your state now?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. does not have a governor.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on your state, and it changes after elections. Look on your state’s official website, or see uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates, which points to official sources. The governor is the head of the executive branch of a state, much as the President is for the nation. Washington, D.C., has no governor; it has a mayor, and saying D.C. has no governor is the right answer there.

questions.q: What is the capital of your state?
a: Answers will vary. [District of Columbia residents should answer that D.C. is not a state and does not have a capital. Residents of U.S. territories should name the capital of the territory.]
questions.idea: This answer depends on where you live. Learn the capital city of your state; your state’s official website lists it. The capital is where the state legislature meets and the governor works. People in D.C. answer that D.C. is not a state; people in a territory name its capital.

questions.q: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them.
a: You don’t have to pay (a poll tax) to vote.
Any citizen can vote. (Women and men can vote.)
A male citizen of any race (can vote).
questions.idea: Four amendments widened the right to vote. The 15th (1870) says the vote cannot be denied because of race, and the 19th (1920) says it cannot be denied because of sex. The 24th (1964) ended poll taxes in federal elections. The 26th (1971) lowered the voting age to 18. Each official answer describes one of these.

questions.q: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?
questions.idea: Some rights belong only to citizens. Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a federal jury. These are both rights and responsibilities of citizenship.

questions.q: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
questions.idea: Many rights in the Constitution protect everyone in the United States, not only citizens. These include freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, freedom to gather peacefully (assembly), freedom to ask the government to fix a problem (petition), and the right to bear arms. Most come from the First and Second Amendments.

questions.q: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
questions.idea: When you say the Pledge of Allegiance, you promise loyalty to the flag and to “the Republic for which it stands,” the United States. The first version was written in 1892 by Francis Bellamy, and Congress made it official in 1942. Saying it is a choice; no one can be forced to say it.

questions.q: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance.
a: Give up loyalty to other countries
Obey the laws of the United States
Serve (help, do important work for) the nation (if needed)
Be loyal to the United States
questions.idea: At the naturalization ceremony, new citizens take the Oath of Allegiance. They promise to give up loyalty to other countries, to support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States, and to be loyal to the United States. They also promise to serve in the military or do important work for the nation if the law requires it.

questions.q: How can people become United States citizens?
a: Be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment
Derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress)
questions.idea: There are three ways. People born in the United States become citizens under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment. Others become citizens by naturalization, the process you are going through. Some children of citizens “derive” citizenship from their parents under laws passed by Congress.

questions.q: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?
a: Give an elected official your opinion (on an issue)
Support or oppose an issue or policy
questions.idea: Civic participation means taking part in public life. Voting is the best known, but people also join political parties or community groups, help with campaigns, contact elected officials, speak up on issues and run for office. Name any two.

questions.q: What is one way Americans can serve their country?
a: Work for local, state, or federal government
questions.idea: Americans serve their country in many ways: by voting, paying taxes, obeying the law, serving in the military, running for office, or working for local, state or federal government. Name any one.

questions.q: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?
a: All people pay to fund the federal government
questions.idea: Taxes pay for the federal government, such as national defense, roads and other services. Paying them is required by law and is a civic duty. The 16th Amendment (1913) gave Congress the power to collect an income tax.

questions.q: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why.
a: Makes the draft fair, if needed
questions.idea: Federal law requires almost all men living in the United States to register with the Selective Service between ages 18 and 25. The list would be used to draft soldiers fairly if Congress ever brought back the draft. There has been no draft since 1973.

questions.q: The colonists came to America for many reasons. Name one.
questions.idea: People came to the colonies for many reasons. Some, like the Pilgrims and Puritans, wanted to worship in their own way. Others wanted land, work or a chance to get ahead. Some were escaping persecution or hard times at home. Memory hook: “faith, freedom and fortune.”

questions.q: Who lived in America before the Europeans arrived?
questions.idea: American Indians, also called Native Americans, lived across North America for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. They formed hundreds of nations with their own languages, governments and ways of life, from the pueblos of the Southwest to the Iroquois Confederacy in the Northeast.

questions.q: What group of people was taken and sold as slaves?
questions.idea: Millions of Africans were captured, taken across the Atlantic Ocean and sold as slaves in the Americas. About 400,000 of them were brought to the land that became the United States. The first enslaved Africans in English Virginia arrived in 1619. Slavery lasted in the United States until the 13th Amendment ended it in 1865.

questions.q: What war did the Americans fight to win independence from Britain?
questions.idea: The American Revolution, or Revolutionary War, was the war the colonists fought against Britain from 1775 to 1783 to win their independence. It ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, when Britain recognized the United States.

questions.q: Name one reason why the Americans declared independence from Britain.
a: British soldiers stayed in Americans’ houses (boarding, quartering)
questions.idea: The colonists were angry that Parliament in Britain taxed them, though they had no representatives there: “no taxation without representation.” Laws like the Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend Acts and Tea Act, the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party and the harsh Intolerable Acts pushed the two sides toward war. Colonists also resented having to house British soldiers. Any one is correct.

questions.q: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?
questions.idea: Thomas Jefferson of Virginia wrote the first draft of the Declaration of Independence in June 1776, when he was 33. A committee that included John Adams and Benjamin Franklin helped, and Congress edited the text before adopting it. Jefferson later became the third President.

questions.q: When was the Declaration of Independence adopted?
questions.idea: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia. That is why Independence Day is July 4. Congress had voted for independence two days earlier, on July 2, and then approved the final words on the 4th.

questions.q: The American Revolution had many important events. Name one.
a: Washington Crossing the Delaware (Battle of Trenton)
questions.idea: Important events of the Revolution include the Battle of Bunker Hill (1775), the Declaration of Independence (1776), Washington crossing the Delaware to win at Trenton (1776), the victory at Saratoga (1777) that brought France into the war, the hard winter at Valley Forge (1777–1778) and the British surrender at Yorktown (1781). Name any one.

questions.q: There were 13 original states. Name five.
questions.idea: The 13 original states were the 13 British colonies along the Atlantic coast. From north to south: New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia. Memory hook: learn them in groups, New England, the middle colonies and the South.

questions.q: What founding document was written in 1787?
questions.idea: The Constitution was written in 1787 at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. It replaced the Articles of Confederation, which had made the national government too weak. It was signed on September 17, 1787, now called Constitution Day.

questions.q: The Federalist Papers supported the passage of the U.S. Constitution. Name one of the writers.
questions.idea: The Federalist Papers were 85 essays written in 1787 and 1788 to persuade New Yorkers to ratify the new Constitution. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay wrote them, and they signed every essay with the same pen name, “Publius.” Any of the four names is an accepted answer.

questions.q: Why were the Federalist Papers important?
a: They helped people understand the (U.S.) Constitution.
questions.idea: The Federalist Papers explained how the new Constitution would work and argued for adopting it. They helped win ratification, and today judges and students still read them to understand what the framers meant.

questions.q: Benjamin Franklin is famous for many things. Name one.
a: Founded the first free public libraries
First Postmaster General of the United States
Helped write the Declaration of Independence
questions.idea: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, writer, scientist and statesman. He helped start an early lending library in Philadelphia, invented the lightning rod and bifocal glasses, was the first Postmaster General, and helped edit the Declaration of Independence. As a diplomat in France, he won French help in the Revolution.

questions.q: George Washington is famous for many things. Name one.
a: First president of the United States
questions.idea: George Washington led the Continental Army in the Revolution, presided over the Constitutional Convention and became the first President (1789–1797). He is called the “Father of Our Country.” His choice to step down after two terms set an example for later Presidents.

questions.q: Thomas Jefferson is famous for many things. Name one.
a: Writer of the Declaration of Independence
Third president of the United States
Doubled the size of the United States (Louisiana Purchase)
Writer of the Virginia Statute on Religious Freedom
questions.idea: Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence and was the first Secretary of State and the third President (1801–1809). As President he made the Louisiana Purchase, which doubled the size of the country. He also wrote the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom and founded the University of Virginia.

questions.q: James Madison is famous for many things. Name one.
a: Fourth president of the United States
One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
questions.idea: James Madison is called the “Father of the Constitution” because he drew up much of the plan for it and kept careful notes at the Convention. He helped write the Federalist Papers and the Bill of Rights, and he was the fourth President, leading the country during the War of 1812.

questions.q: Alexander Hamilton is famous for many things. Name one.
a: One of the writers of the Federalist Papers
Helped establish the First Bank of the United States
questions.idea: Alexander Hamilton was an aide to General Washington in the Revolution, a member of the Continental Congress and a writer of most of the Federalist Papers. As the first Secretary of the Treasury, he set up the nation’s finances and helped create the First Bank of the United States. His face is on the ten-dollar bill.

questions.q: What territory did the United States buy from France in 1803?
questions.idea: In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from France for about $15 million. It was a huge area west of the Mississippi River, and it roughly doubled the size of the country. President Thomas Jefferson then sent Lewis and Clark to explore it.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1800s.
questions.idea: The United States fought four wars on the list in the 1800s: the War of 1812 with Britain, the Mexican-American War (1846–1848), the Civil War (1861–1865) and the Spanish-American War (1898). Memory hook: one war with Britain, one with Mexico, one at home, one with Spain.

questions.q: Name the U.S. war between the North and the South.
questions.idea: The Civil War (1861–1865) was fought between the Union, the Northern states, and the Confederacy, eleven Southern states that had tried to leave the Union. The main issue was slavery. The Union won, the country stayed together, and slavery was ended.

questions.q: The Civil War had many important events. Name one.
questions.idea: Key events of the Civil War include the attack on Fort Sumter (1861), which began the war; the Battle of Antietam (1862); the Emancipation Proclamation (1863); the Union victories at Gettysburg and Vicksburg (1863); Sherman’s March through Georgia (1864); the surrender at Appomattox (1865); and the assassination of President Lincoln (1865). Name any one.

questions.q: Abraham Lincoln is famous for many things. Name one.
a: Led the United States during the Civil War
questions.idea: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President. He led the Union through the Civil War, preserved the Union, issued the Emancipation Proclamation and gave the Gettysburg Address. He was assassinated in April 1865, just days after the war’s main Confederate army surrendered.

questions.q: What did the Emancipation Proclamation do?
a: Freed slaves in the Confederate states
Freed slaves in most Southern states
questions.idea: President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War. It declared enslaved people free in the states that were fighting against the Union. It did not free enslaved people in border states that stayed loyal; the 13th Amendment (1865) ended slavery everywhere in the country.

questions.q: What U.S. war ended slavery?
questions.idea: The Civil War ended slavery in the United States. The Union victory made it possible to pass the 13th Amendment in 1865, which abolished slavery everywhere in the country.

questions.q: What amendment says all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are U.S. citizens?
questions.idea: The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 after the Civil War, says that people born or naturalized in the United States and subject to its laws are citizens. It made formerly enslaved people citizens, and it also promises equal protection of the laws.

questions.q: When did all men get the right to vote?
questions.idea: After the Civil War, during Reconstruction, the 15th Amendment (1870) said the right to vote could not be denied because of race. In practice many Black men were later kept from voting by poll taxes, literacy tests and violence, until the civil rights laws of the 1960s. Women gained the vote nationally in 1920.

questions.q: Name one leader of the women’s rights movement in the 1800s.
questions.idea: In the 1800s, women and men organized to win rights for women, including the right to vote. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848; Susan B. Anthony and Lucy Stone led suffrage groups. Sojourner Truth and Harriet Tubman, who had escaped slavery, spoke for both abolition and women’s rights.

questions.q: Name one war fought by the United States in the 1900s.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The United States fought in five wars on this list in the 1900s: World War I (1917–1918), World War II (1941–1945), the Korean War (1950–1953), the Vietnam War, and the Persian Gulf War (1991). Any one of them is a correct answer.

questions.q: Why did the United States enter World War I?
a: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, Italy, and Russia)
To oppose the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria)
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The United States stayed neutral when World War I began in 1914. It entered in April 1917 after German submarines attacked ships carrying Americans, and after Germany asked Mexico to join a war against the United States. The United States fought on the side of the Allies against the Central Powers.

questions.q: When did all women get the right to vote?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Women across the country won the right to vote in 1920, when the 19th Amendment was ratified, right after World War I. It followed more than 70 years of work by the women’s suffrage movement. Some states had already let women vote before then.

questions.q: What was the Great Depression?
a: Longest economic recession in modern history
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The Great Depression was the worst and longest economic downturn in modern American history. It lasted through the 1930s. At its worst, about one worker in four had no job, many banks failed and many families lost homes and farms.

questions.q: When did the Great Depression start?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The Great Depression began with the stock market crash of October 1929, often called the Great Crash. Stock prices fell sharply, and the shock spread to banks, businesses and jobs.

questions.q: Who was president during the Great Depression and World War II?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Franklin D. Roosevelt was President from 1933 to 1945, through most of the Great Depression and most of World War II. He is the only President elected four times. After him, the 22nd Amendment limited Presidents to two elected terms.

questions.q: Why did the United States enter World War II?
a: To support the Allied Powers (England, France, and Russia)
To oppose the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, and Japan)
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. The next day the United States declared war on Japan, and Germany and Italy soon declared war on the United States. America then fought with the Allies against the Axis Powers.

questions.q: Dwight Eisenhower is famous for many things. Name one.
a: President at the end of (during) the Korean War
Signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 (Created the Interstate System)
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Dwight D. Eisenhower commanded the Allied forces in Europe in World War II, including the D-Day landings in 1944. He was the 34th President (1953–1961); a cease-fire ended the fighting in Korea early in his first term, and in 1956 he signed the law that built the Interstate Highway System.

questions.q: Who was the United States’ main rival during the Cold War?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: During the Cold War, from the late 1940s to 1991, the main rival of the United States was the Soviet Union, also called the USSR. Russia was its largest part, so “Russia” is also accepted. The two sides never fought a full war directly, which is why it is called “cold.”

questions.q: During the Cold War, what was one main concern of the United States?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: During the Cold War, Americans worried that communism would spread to more countries, and that a conflict with the Soviet Union could lead to nuclear war. The U.S. policy of trying to stop communism from spreading was called containment.

questions.q: Why did the United States enter the Korean War?
a: To stop the spread of communism
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: In 1950 communist North Korea invaded South Korea. The United States, with the United Nations, sent troops to defend the South and stop the spread of communism. The fighting ended with an armistice in 1953, and Korea is still divided.

questions.q: Why did the United States enter the Vietnam War?
a: To stop the spread of communism
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The United States sent aid and then troops to help South Vietnam against communist North Vietnam, to stop the spread of communism in Southeast Asia. American combat troops left in 1973, and North Vietnam took over the South in 1975.

questions.q: What did the civil rights movement do?
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: The civil rights movement worked to end racial discrimination and segregation, especially against Black Americans. Through court cases, peaceful protests, boycotts and marches, it won major laws in the 1960s, such as the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

questions.q: Martin Luther King, Jr. is famous for many things. Name one.
a: Worked for equality for all Americans
Worked to ensure that people would “not be judged by the color of their skin, but by the content of their character”
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Martin Luther King, Jr. was a minister and a leader of the civil rights movement who taught peaceful, nonviolent protest. In his “I Have a Dream” speech in 1963, he hoped his children would be judged by their character, not the color of their skin. He was killed in 1968, and a national holiday honors him.

questions.q: Why did the United States enter the Persian Gulf War?
a: To force the Iraqi military from Kuwait
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: In August 1990, Iraq invaded its small neighbor Kuwait. In early 1991 the United States led a coalition of many countries that forced the Iraqi military out of Kuwait. The war was short; the ground fighting lasted about 100 hours.

questions.q: What major event happened on September 11, 2001 in the United States?
a: Terrorists took over two planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center in New York City
Terrorists took over a plane and crashed into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia
Terrorists took over a plane originally aimed at Washington, D.C., and crashed in a field in Pennsylvania
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: On September 11, 2001, terrorists took over four passenger planes. Two hit the World Trade Center in New York City, one hit the Pentagon near Washington, D.C., and one crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. Nearly 3,000 people were killed. It was the deadliest attack on American soil in the nation’s history.

questions.q: Name one U.S. military conflict after the September 11, 2001 attacks.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: After the attacks of September 11, 2001, the United States began what it called the Global War on Terror. This included the war in Afghanistan, which began in 2001, and the war in Iraq, which began in 2003. Name any one.

questions.q: Name one American Indian tribe in the United States.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.note: For a complete list of tribes, please visit bia.gov.
questions.idea: There are hundreds of American Indian tribes in the United States; the federal government recognizes more than 570 of them as nations with their own governments. Any tribe on the list is an accepted answer. Pick one name you can say with confidence, such as Cherokee, Navajo or Sioux. The Bureau of Indian Affairs, at bia.gov, keeps the full list.

questions.q: Name one example of an American innovation.
questions.part: C: Recent American History and Other Important Historical Information
questions.idea: Americans have created many inventions. Thomas Edison’s team made a practical light bulb (1879); the Wright brothers flew the first airplane (1903); Henry Ford’s moving assembly line made cars cheaper (1913); American engineers invented the integrated circuit, or computer chip (1958); and Americans first landed on the moon (1969). Name any one.

questions.q: What is the capital of the United States?
questions.idea: Washington, D.C., is the capital of the United States. “D.C.” stands for District of Columbia, a federal district that is not part of any state. The Constitution allowed for such a district, and the government moved there in 1800. The city is named for George Washington.

questions.q: Where is the Statue of Liberty?
a: Liberty Island [Also acceptable are New Jersey, near New York City, and on the Hudson (River).]
questions.idea: The Statue of Liberty stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor, close to the New Jersey shore; that is why New Jersey and the Hudson River are also accepted. It was a gift from the people of France and was dedicated in 1886. For millions of immigrants arriving by ship, it was one of the first sights of America.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
a: (Because the stripes) represent the original colonies
questions.idea: The flag has 13 stripes, 7 red and 6 white, for the 13 original colonies that became the first states. Memory hook: the stripes look back to the beginning; the stars count the states today.

questions.q: Why does the flag have 50 stars?
a: (Because there is) one star for each state
questions.idea: The flag has 50 stars, one for each state. A new star is added on the Fourth of July after a state joins. The 50-star flag has flown since July 4, 1960, after Hawaii became the 50th state.

questions.q: What is the name of the national anthem?
questions.idea: The national anthem is “The Star-Spangled Banner.” Francis Scott Key wrote the words in 1814 after watching the British attack Fort McHenry in Baltimore during the War of 1812. In the morning he saw the American flag still flying. Congress made it the national anthem in 1931.

questions.q: The Nation’s first motto was “E Pluribus Unum.” What does that mean?
questions.idea: “E Pluribus Unum” is Latin for “Out of many, one.” It first meant that many states form one nation; today many people also take it to mean that people from many places become one people. It is on the Great Seal of the United States and on coins. “In God We Trust” became the official national motto in 1956.

questions.q: What is Independence Day?
a: A holiday to celebrate U.S. independence (from Britain)
questions.idea: Independence Day, July 4, celebrates the adoption of the Declaration of Independence in 1776. It is the country’s birthday. Americans mark it with parades, picnics and fireworks.

questions.q: Name three national U.S. holidays.
questions.idea: There are eleven federal holidays: New Year’s Day, Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Presidents Day (Washington’s Birthday), Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas. Juneteenth, the newest, marks June 19, 1865, when news of freedom reached enslaved people in Galveston, Texas. Name any three.

questions.q: What is Memorial Day?
a: A holiday to honor soldiers who died in military service
questions.idea: Memorial Day, the last Monday in May, honors the men and women who died while serving in the U.S. military. Memory hook: Memorial Day remembers those who died; Veterans Day thanks all who served.

questions.q: What is Veterans Day?
a: A holiday to honor people in the (U.S.) military
A holiday to honor people who have served (in the U.S. military)
questions.idea: Veterans Day, November 11, honors everyone who has served in the U.S. armed forces, living or dead. The date marks the armistice that ended the fighting of World War I in 1918.

ideas: “The idea behind it” (idea, ladder) is original Teddy Rook Book writing, not part of the USCIS list; it never names current officeholders.
